Multidimensional arrays

Source: vignettes/articles/multidim.Rmd
multidim.Rmd

GDAL has two models of a raster. The classic one is a stack of two-dimensional bands, and a netCDF or Zarr variable with a time or depth axis reaches it as hundreds of subdatasets or bands, with the axes flattened into names. The multidimensional model, added in GDAL 3.1, keeps the source’s own shape: groups that hold arrays, arrays that have named dimensions, dimensions that have coordinate variables, and attributes everywhere.

GDAL7 binds the multidimensional model directly, as S7 classes with properties, in the same way as the classic one. Nothing is translated through the classic model on the way, and nothing is read until it is asked for. This article walks through it with a small Zarr store that ships with the package, so every line below runs as written.

library(GDAL7)
path <- system.file("extdata/multidim.zarr", package = "GDAL7")

Opening: the same file, two models

Opened the classic way, the Zarr store is a dataset whose array has become bands:

classic <- gdal_open(path)
classic@raster_count
#> [1] 3
gdal_close(classic)

Opened with multidim = TRUE, it is a tree. The root group is the way in:

ds <- gdal_open(path, multidim = TRUE)
root <- get_root_group(ds)
root
#> <GDALGroup>
#>   Name: /
#>   Arrays (4): lon, temperature, lat, time
root@mdarray_names
#> [1] "lon"         "temperature" "lat"         "time"
root@group_names
#> character(0)

A group’s arrays are opened by name, and a deeper one by its full path from the root, such as "/ocean/temperature". Subgroups are opened with open_group().

temperature <- open_mdarray(root, "temperature")
temperature
#> <GDALMDArray>
#>   Name: temperature
#>   Type: Float64
#>   Dimensions: time=3, lat=4, lon=5
#>   Unit: degC
#>   NoData: -999

What an array knows about itself

Everything an array says about itself is a property, read from GDAL when it is asked for. mdarray_info() collects the lot in one call:

str(mdarray_info(temperature))
#> List of 10
#>  $ name      : chr "temperature"
#>  $ full_name : chr "/temperature"
#>  $ data_type : chr "Float64"
#>  $ unit      : chr "degC"
#>  $ nodata    : num -999
#>  $ scale     : num 2
#>  $ offset    : num 0.5
#>  $ crs       : chr NA
#>  $ dimensions:'data.frame':  3 obs. of  5 variables:
#>   ..$ name     : chr [1:3] "time" "lat" "lon"
#>   ..$ size     : num [1:3] 3 4 5
#>   ..$ type     : chr [1:3] "TEMPORAL" "HORIZONTAL_Y" "HORIZONTAL_X"
#>   ..$ direction: chr [1:3] "" "NORTH" "EAST"
#>   ..$ indexed  : logi [1:3] TRUE TRUE TRUE
#>  $ attributes:List of 3
#>   ..$ coordinates: chr "lat lon"
#>   ..$ long_name  : chr "air temperature"
#>   ..$ valid_range: num [1:2] -50 50

The dimensions are a data frame, in GDAL’s order, slowest varying first. That is the order the format declares them in and the order gdal mdim info prints:

temperature@dimensions
#>   name size         type direction indexed
#> 1 time    3     TEMPORAL              TRUE
#> 2  lat    4 HORIZONTAL_Y     NORTH    TRUE
#> 3  lon    5 HORIZONTAL_X      EAST    TRUE

type and direction are what the format says about each dimension, and they are how GDAL picks the X and Y of a raster later on. indexed says whether the dimension has a coordinate variable, and dimension_values reads them all:

temperature@dimension_values
#> $time
#> [1] 0 1 2
#> 
#> $lat
#> [1] -40 -41 -42 -43
#> 
#> $lon
#> [1] 140 141 142 143 144

coordinate_variables is the related, more general question: which arrays the format names as this one’s coordinates. For a regular grid the answer is the same arrays; for a swath it is two-dimensional latitude and longitude arrays that index no dimension.

vapply(temperature@coordinate_variables, function(x) x@name, "")
#> [1] "lat" "lon"

The array’s own annotations are in attributes, and the ones GDAL interprets have properties of their own:

temperature@attributes
#> $coordinates
#> [1] "lat lon"
#> 
#> $long_name
#> [1] "air temperature"
#> 
#> $valid_range
#> [1] -50  50
temperature@unit_type
#> [1] "degC"
temperature@nodata_value
#> [1] -999
c(scale = temperature@scale, offset = temperature@offset)
#>  scale offset 
#>    2.0    0.5

Reading

read_mdarray() with no arguments reads the whole array:

values <- read_mdarray(temperature)
dim(values)
#>  lon  lat time 
#>    5    4    3
values[, , 1]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1    6   11   16
#> [2,]    2    7   12   17
#> [3,]    3   NA   13   18
#> [4,]    4    9   14   19
#> [5,]    5   10   15   20

The result’s dim is the reverse of the array’s dimension order, so a (time, lat, lon) array reads into [lon, lat, time]. That is the order ncdf4 and RNetCDF give, and it is the order the values arrive in from GDAL, so the buffer becomes the R array with nothing moved. The names on dim say which is which.

The nodata value, here -999, has become NA; nodata_as_na = FALSE keeps it. The scale and offset are not applied: the values are the stored ones, and the physical ones are a step away:

range(values * temperature@scale + temperature@offset, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1]   2.5 120.5

A read can be a hyperslab: an origin, a count along each dimension, and a step. All three are in GDAL’s dimension order, with the origin counting from 1 as R does. The second time step, every second longitude:

read_mdarray(temperature, start = c(2, 1, 1), count = c(1, 4, 3),
             step = c(1, 1, 2))
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]   21   26   31   36
#> [2,]   23   28   33   38
#> [3,]   25   30   35   40

A negative step reads backwards. Latitude in this array runs from -40 to -43; reading it the other way round puts the south first:

read_mdarray(temperature, start = c(1, 4, 1), count = c(1, 4, 5),
             step = c(1, -1, 1))
#> , , 1
#> 
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]   16   11    6    1
#> [2,]   17   12    7    2
#> [3,]   18   13   NA    3
#> [4,]   19   14    9    4
#> [5,]   20   15   10    5

Views

A view is a slice, a reordering or a transposition in GDAL’s own syntax, modelled on numpy’s. It reads nothing; it is another GDALMDArray, with the same properties, that reads through to the original. Indices in a view count from 0, as they do in GDAL:

first <- get_view(temperature, "[0,:,:]")
first@dimensions
#>   name size         type direction indexed
#> 1  lat    4 HORIZONTAL_Y     NORTH    TRUE
#> 2  lon    5 HORIZONTAL_X      EAST    TRUE

flipped <- get_view(temperature, "[:,::-1,:]")
flipped@dimensions$name
#> [1] "time"              "subset_lat_3_-1_4" "lon"
flipped@dimension_values[[2]]
#> [1] -43 -42 -41 -40

A sliced dimension is renamed to say what was done to it, as above, and its coordinate variable is sliced with it.

A view can be taken of a view, and a dimension is dropped by indexing it with a single number, as [0,:,:] does to time. A range is start:stop:step, with stop excluded as in Python, so "[:,0:2,1:5:2]" is the first two latitudes and every second longitude from the second.

Back to a classic raster

A two-dimensional array is a raster, and as_classic_dataset() turns one into a GDALDataset, so the rest of the package applies to it. The geotransform is worked out from the coordinate variables:

slice <- as_classic_dataset(first)
slice@geotransform
#>        origin_x     pixel_width    row_rotation        origin_y column_rotation 
#>           139.5             1.0             0.0           -39.5             0.0 
#>    pixel_height 
#>            -1.0
c(slice@raster_xsize, slice@raster_ysize)
#> [1] 5 4
matrix(read_raster(slice)[[1]], slice@raster_xsize)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1    6   11   16
#> [2,]    2    7   12   17
#> [3,]    3 -999   13   18
#> [4,]    4    9   14   19
#> [5,]    5   10   15   20

read_raster() gives the band’s stored values, nodata included, in the order read_mdarray() would: X fastest.

X and Y are chosen from the dimensions’ type, falling back to the last two dimensions; x_dim and y_dim say otherwise. The reverse direction is as_mdarray(), which presents a classic band as a two-dimensional array.

Chunks

A chunked store is fastest read a whole chunk at a time, and block_size is the chunk shape, in GDAL’s order. This store has one time step per chunk:

temperature@block_size
#> time  lat  lon 
#>    1    4    5

advise_read() tells the driver what is about to be read. For Zarr that means every chunk in the slice is fetched and decoded on GDAL’s threads at once, rather than one after the other as the read reaches it. It matters most for a remote store, where each chunk is a request:

advise_read(temperature, start = c(1, 1, 1), count = c(3, 4, 5))
dim(read_mdarray(temperature, start = c(1, 1, 1), count = c(3, 4, 5)))
#>  lon  lat time 
#>    5    4    3

With the altarr package installed, as_altarr() makes a lazy R array that reads chunks only when they are indexed, in batches, with each batch advised first. Built from a path, it keeps the path and opens the dataset on its first read, in this session or a later one:

lazy <- as_altarr(path, array = "temperature")
dim(lazy)
#> [1] 5 4 3
lazy[, , 3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]   41   46   51   56
#> [2,]   42   47   52   57
#> [3,]   43   48   53   58
#> [4,]   44   49   54   59
#> [5,]   45   50   55   60

GDAL’s multidimensional programs

gdal mdim info, convert, mosaic and the rest are algorithms in GDAL’s registry, and gdal_run() runs them; gdal_algorithms("mdim") lists what this GDAL has. They need GDAL 3.11 for the registry and 3.12 for mosaic, so the code here asks first:

has_mosaic <- gdal_has_algorithms() && "mosaic" %in% gdal_algorithms("mdim")
has_mosaic
#> [1] TRUE
report <- gdal_run("mdim info", list(input = path), progress = FALSE)
cat(substr(report, 1, 300), "...\n")
#> {
#>   "type": "group",
#>   "driver": "Zarr",
#>   "name": "/",
#>   "dimensions": [
#>     {
#>       "name": "lat",
#>       "full_name": "/lat",
#>       "size": 4,
#>       "type": "HORIZONTAL_Y",
#>       "direction": "NORTH",
#>       "indexing_variable": "/lat"
#>     },
#>     {
#>       "name": "lon",
#>       "full_name": "/lon",
#>    ...

A mosaic puts back together an array that was split into files, which is how a long model run is usually published: one file per month, or per day. To show it here the store is first split into one Zarr per time step with gdal mdim convert:

dir <- tempfile()
dir.create(dir)
pieces <- character(0)
for (t in 0:2) {
  piece <- file.path(dir, sprintf("step%d.zarr", t))
  gdal_run("mdim convert", list(
    input = path, output = piece, "output-format" = "Zarr",
    subset = sprintf("time(%d,%d)", t, t)
  ), progress = FALSE)
  pieces <- c(pieces, piece)
}
basename(pieces)
#> [1] "step0.zarr" "step1.zarr" "step2.zarr"

gdal mdim mosaic then writes a multidimensional VRT that stitches them back together along time. The VRT is a small XML file that holds no values, only where each piece goes:

vrt <- file.path(dir, "mosaic.vrt")
gdal_run("mdim mosaic", list(input = pieces, output = vrt), progress = FALSE)

mosaic <- gdal_open(vrt, multidim = TRUE)
stitched <- open_mdarray(get_root_group(mosaic), "temperature")
stitched@dimensions
#>   name size type direction indexed
#> 1 time    3                   TRUE
#> 2  lat    4                   TRUE
#> 3  lon    5                   TRUE
identical(read_mdarray(stitched), values)
#> [1] TRUE

The same values, read from three files through one array, and the files were not copied: the VRT points at them. The same can be done with files on a web server or object storage through /vsicurl/ or /vsis3/ paths, which is how a model run published one file per month becomes one array.
